title: Twenty identical coins, one winner
hook: Flip 20 fair coins 20 times each. Is the coin with the most heads special?

knows: a fair coin gives heads half the time on average
results vary by luck from try to try
doesNotKnow: that picking the best of many noisy results inflates its score
that the winner's next result falls back toward the truth

misconception: The top performer of a group looks best because it is best, so its score should repeat.
objective: The learner can explain that among 20 identical fair coins the winner averages about 14 heads in 20 by luck alone, and the same coin flipped again averages about 10.
keyState: First winner (14 heads) re-flipped (12), then 101 contests: winners averaged 14.1, their re-flips 9.6.

claims.text: Among 20 fair coins each flipped 20 times, the coin with the most heads gets about 14 heads on average.
claims.source: E[max of 20 independent Bin(20, 1/2)] = sum_k k (F(k)^20 - F(k-1)^20) = 14.116 (exactMax() in src/demos/probability/best-of-twenty-identical/model.ts; brief said 14.12). Options 10 / 12 / 14 are FLIPS/2, FLIPS/2 + 2 and round(exactMax()).

claims.text: On the stage, the first contest's winner got 14 heads and, flipped again, 12; over 101 contests the winners averaged 14.1 heads and their re-flips 9.6.
claims.source: contests() in model.ts, mulberry32 seed 314, untuned (the first seed tried); winner = first coin with the highest count. Over seeds 1-1000 the 101-contest winner average had middle 95% 13.9-14.3 (median 14.1) and the re-flip average 9.6-10.5 (median 10.0); seed 314's 9.6 is at the low edge.

claims.text: Any fair coin flipped 20 times gives 10 heads on average, so the winner's re-flip averages 10.
claims.source: E[Bin(20, 1/2)] = 10; the re-flip is independent of the contest.

claims.text: Picking the top of many noisy scores picks the luckiest; its next result falls back toward the truth (the winner's curse).
claims.source: All 20 coins are identical (c1, c3): the winner's excess over 10 is pure selection on noise. Term: Thaler, R. (1988), 'Anomalies: The Winner's Curse', Journal of Economic Perspectives 2(1): 191-202 (auction origin; used here in its selection-on-noise sense).

recall.question: Of 50 fund managers who all pick stocks at random, the best one beat the market by 15% last year. What do you expect from them next year?
options: About the same as a random manager
recall.why: If all 50 are equally random, the top score was luck. Picked for luck, the winner falls back to what any random picker gets.
